stops.name: Villa Rica, the ships given to the través
stops.campa: With mutiny brewing among Velázquez loyalists eager to sail home, Cortés's own captains counsel the master stroke: sink the fleet. On his order, or with his captains' full complicity, as Bernal Díaz insists, so that the courage and the blame are shared, the pilots run all but one ship aground and strip them of iron, sail-cloth, and rigging for the army's own use before the hulls settle into the sand. Two hundred and fifty men and every heart in the company now face one road only: forward, to the city in the lake they have heard of and not yet seen.
stops.quote: que no dejase navío ninguno en el puerto, sino que luego diese al través con todos.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 58

stops.name: Tlaxcala, the hard alliance
stops.campa: The army climbs from the coast through cold pine country into the lands of Tlaxcala, ancient enemy of the Aztec confederation, whose warriors under young Xicohténcatl test the Spaniards in three hard battles before the elder lords, Maxixcatzin, Xicohténcatl the elder, decide the strangers are worth more as allies than as corpses. They open their city, feed the starving column, and give women in the custom that seals a pact between houses. From this hour Cortés commands not five hundred Spaniards but an army of thousands of Tlaxcaltecas, whose hatred of Tenochtitlan will do more to bring it down than any Spanish sword.

stops.name: Cholula, the massacre
stops.campa: At Cholula, sacred city of Quetzalcoatl and Moctezuma's wary ally, the welcome sours within days: food stops arriving, the streets are found barricaded, and Doña Marina hears from a cholulteca woman of a plan to trap the column in the narrow lanes with an Aztec force said to wait beyond the town. Cortés summons the lords to the temple courtyard on pretext of departure and, at a signal, his men and thousands of Tlaxcalteca allies fall on the unarmed gathering. Between four and six thousand die within hours. Whether the ambush was real or invented, the massacre's message reaches every town between here and the lake.

stops.name: Paso de Cortés, between the volcanoes
stops.campa: Against Moctezuma's own advice, sent by envoys who describe an impassable road guarded by demons, Cortés chooses the harder, higher route between the two great snow volcanoes, Popocatépetl smoking and Iztaccíhuatl the sleeping woman beside him. Diego de Ordaz climbs partway up the smoking cone out of pure curiosity and is the first European to see its crater, a feat the Emperor will later let him wear on his own coat of arms. From the saddle between the peaks the army gets its first sight of the Valley of Mexico entire: the lake, the causeways, a white city standing on the water like something painted.

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the causeway meeting with Moctezuma
stops.campa: Down the causeway from Iztapalapa, between lake and lake, the column of Spaniards and Tlaxcaltecas advances on a city of tens of thousands of houses ringed by water, and the soldiers murmur that it is like the enchantments told in the book of Amadís, and wonder aloud if they dream. At the causeway's meeting-point Moctezuma himself comes out under a canopy of green feathers and gold, borne by lords who will not meet his eye, to receive the strangers as guests in his father's palace: the last free morning of an empire, given away, the canon insists, at its own door.
stops.quote: Y desde que vimos tantas ciudades y villas pobladas en el agua, y en tierra firme otras grandes poblaciones, y aquella calzada tan derecha y por nivel como iba a México, nos quedamos admirados y decíamos que parecía a las cosas de encantamiento que se cuentan en el libro de Amadís.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 87

stops.name: The palace of Axayácatl, the seizure of Moctezuma
stops.campa: Lodged in the palace of Moctezuma's father Axayácatl, Cortés within a week turns guest into gaoler: on news that a garrison at Vera Cruz has been attacked and a Spaniard killed on the coast, he walks into the emperor's presence with his captains and, after long and courteous argument, has him moved, walking, unchained, but never again free, into the Spanish quarters. Moctezuma governs the empire from captivity for months, orders his own coastal chiefs burned for the killing, and delivers gold, feather-work, and turquoise beyond counting, melted into bars stamped with the royal fifth before men already dreaming of Spain.

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the massacre at the Toxcatl festival
stops.campa: In Cortés's absence, Pedro de Alvarado, left in command of a small garrison, grows certain, rightly, or from fear alone, the canon leaves it open, that the dancers gathered unarmed in the Great Temple's courtyard for the feast of Toxcatl mean an ambush of his own. He seals the exits and puts his men to the sword among drums and flower garlands; hundreds of the Mexica nobility die inside the temple walls they cannot leave. The city that has watched its emperor become a captive without rising now rises, and news reaches Cortés on the coast that Tenochtitlan has closed like a fist around his garrison.
stops.quote: Hay en esta gran ciudad muchas mezquitas o casas de sus ídolos de muy hermosos edificios por las colaciones y barrios de ella.
stops.quote_source: Hernán Cortés, Segunda Carta de Relación (1520)

stops.name: Cempoala, Narváez defeated
stops.campa: Velázquez, furious at the upstart who defied him, sends Pánfilo de Narváez with nineteen ships and more men than Cortés has ever commanded, to arrest him and seize New Spain outright. Cortés marches from the lake by forced stages, out-talks Narváez's own captains into desertion with promised gold, and falls on the larger camp at Cempoala in a night attack through drenching rain. A pikeman puts out Narváez's eye in the first rush; he is captured shouting that he has been beaten, and his whole army, offered pay and plunder, changes coats within the week and marches inland as Cortés's own.

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the death of Moctezuma
stops.campa: Besieged in the palace, starving, water and food cut off, Cortés brings Moctezuma to the rooftop to calm his own people, and the emperor is answered with stones and arrows by subjects who no longer call him lord. Some say his own successor's men strike him down for the shame of it, some say Spanish hands finish what the stones began. He dies of his wounds within days, the last tlatoani to rule the old way, and with him dies the fiction that has kept the Spaniards alive inside a hostile city: that the Mexica still had, however captive, an emperor to obey.

stops.name: The Noche Triste, flight down the Tacuba causeway
stops.campa: At midnight, in rain, the garrison steals out along the Tacuba causeway carrying a portable bridge and every man's private fortune in gold sewn into his clothes. Those loyal to Cortés take little and travel light; Narváez's men, greedy to the end, load themselves with treasure and drown in it. A woman grinding maize sees them and cries the alarm; canoes swarm the lake on both sides, the bridge fails at the second gap, and men, horses, and cannon go into the water together, the night filling with cries for help that no one can answer.
stops.quote: De los muchos que se ahogaban, ellos y los caballos, y de otros muchos soldados que allí en el agua mataban y metían en las canoas, que era muy gran lástima de lo ver y oír, pues la grita y lloros y lástimas que decían demandando socorro.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 128

stops.name: Popotla, the tree where he wept
stops.campa: At dawn, clear of the lake at last on the dry ground of Popotla, Cortés gathers what remains of an army that entered the city eight months ago whole: a third of the Spaniards dead or captured for sacrifice, the Tlaxcalteca dead by the thousand, every cannon and most of the gold gone into the lake. Tradition, not Cortés's own letter, which says nothing of it, but the memory the country keeps, sets him down beneath an ancient ahuehuete on the causeway's end, head bowed, unable any longer to hide the tears the disaster has cost him. The tree stands in Popotla still, and the night keeps his name.

stops.name: Otumba, the battle turned by the standard
stops.campa: Six days of retreat through hostile towns, wounded and starving, bring the column onto the open plain of Otumba where the massed levies of the valley, tens of thousands, by every account, against a few hundred Spaniards on foot, close in to finish what the causeway began. Cortés, seeing the battle turning against exhausted men, drives with a handful of horsemen straight for the enemy's commanding general, recognizable by his quetzal-feather standard and cotton armor, and cuts him down with a lance-thrust; the standard falls, and an army that fights by omen and rank breaks apart at the sign and scatters. The road to Tlaxcala opens behind the rout.
